title: Saaz Hops and Czech Lager | Craft Beer School
desc: Why Saaz hops define Czech pale lager: the variety, its low alpha and spicy aroma, how Czech brewers use it and what that means on a commercial brewhouse.
teaser: Czech pale lager tastes of soft water, rich malt and a lot of Saaz. The hop is gentle, which is exactly why brewers use so much of it.
standfirst: Saaz is the classic hop of Czech pale lager. It is low in alpha acid and quietly spicy rather than loud. Understanding why Czech brewers use it the way they do explains a lot about the style.
sections: Saaz is a landrace hop from northwest Bohemia

Saaz takes its name from the German name for Žatec, a town in northwest Bohemia in the Czech Republic. Hops have been grown in the region for centuries. Saaz is one of the four traditional noble hops, alongside Hallertau Mittelfrüh, Tettnang and Spalt. Our guide to noble hops covers the group.

Saaz is low in alpha acid, typically around 2.5 to 4.5%. Its cohumulone share is low too, often around 23 to 28% of total alpha. The oil profile is what sets it apart: modest myrcene and a high share of farnesene, which is unusual among hops. Brewers describe the aroma as spicy, herbal, peppery and earthy, with a soft floral note.
Czech pale lager was built around it

The first pale lager of the Pilsner type was brewed in Plzeň in 1842. It combined pale malt, very soft local water, bottom-fermenting yeast and Saaz hops. That combination became the model for pale lagers around the world.

A Czech premium pale lager today is golden and full flavoured. Bitterness is firm, often around 30 to 45 IBU, but the very soft water keeps it rounded rather than sharp. The malt is rich and bready, sometimes with a touch of caramel from decoction mashing. Saaz sits on top: spicy, floral and clean. Our guide to Czech versus German Pilsner sets out the differences in detail.
Low alpha means a lot of hop material

Reaching 35 IBU with a 3.5% alpha hop takes a large amount of hops. Roughly three to four times the weight you would need with a 12% alpha hop. That is not only a cost issue. All that plant material brings polyphenols and other compounds into the wort as well as alpha acids.

Many brewers think this is part of the Czech character. The bitterness feels fuller and softer than the same IBU from a small dose of high-alpha hops. Swap Saaz for a high-alpha bittering hop and the beer changes, even with the same calculated bitterness. It is one reason Czech-style brewers often use Saaz for every addition, not just the late ones.
Czech brewers spread additions through the boil

Traditional Czech practice uses several Saaz additions, often three, spread across a long boil. A common pattern puts the largest share early for bitterness, a second addition in the middle and a final addition near the end for aroma. Some brewers add a first wort hop as well. Dry hopping is not traditional in Czech pale lager, though some modern breweries do it lightly.

On a 1,000 litre batch at 12 °P and 35 IBU, that can mean several kilograms of Saaz pellets. Plan the kettle and the whirlpool for that load of hop matter. More trub means more wort loss, so allow for it in your volumes.
Soft water and decoction complete the picture

Plzeň water is famously soft, with very low mineral content. High-sulphate water and Saaz make a harsh, coarse beer. Many Indian breweries start from borewell water with high hardness and alkalinity, so reverse osmosis (RO) water with small calcium chloride additions is the usual route to a Czech profile.

Decoction mashing, where part of the mash is boiled and returned, is traditional too. It builds a richer malt character and darker colour. Our guide to decoction mashing covers the method. Czech beers are also traditionally named by original gravity: a desítka at 10 °P and a dvanáctka at 12 °P.
Freshness matters more with delicate hops

Saaz aroma is subtle, so it suffers from ageing more visibly than bold modern hops. A tired lot tastes flat and cheesy rather than spicy. Store pellets frozen and check the harvest year and the hop storage index on the certificate. In India, where the hops arrive after a long journey, insist on cold transport and inspect the packs on arrival.

Here is the floor detail: Czech lager rewards a long, cold lagering of four weeks or more around 0 to 2 °C. That lets the hop character settle and the bitterness round out. Rushing it to the tap in ten days gives you a different beer.
The style is a lesson in balance

Czech pale lager shows how hop variety, water, malt and mash interact. Change one and the beer moves. That interaction is what makes it a good style to learn brewing science on. The recipe alone will not tell you why Saaz tastes softer at the same IBU or why hard water ruins it.
Smell Saaz against a modern hop

Rub a few pellets of Saaz between your palms next to a high-alpha American hop. Note the difference in intensity and character. Then taste a fresh Czech pale lager and look for that same spice in the finish.
faqs: Spicy, herbal, peppery and earthy, with a soft floral note. It is subtle rather than loud.
What is the alpha acid of Saaz?
Typically around 2.5 to 4.5%, which is low. Brewers need a large weight of Saaz to reach normal lager bitterness.
Yes. It is one of the four traditional noble hops alongside Hallertau Mittelfrüh, Tettnang and Spalt.
What water suits Czech pale lager?
Very soft water with low mineral content. Hard or high-sulphate water makes Saaz bitterness harsh.
